speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT USE OF ANIMAL STEEL LEG TRAPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not trapped, but I would like to take part in the interesting debate on my hon. colleague's Bill C-221, through which he would like to amend the Criminal Code so as to punish those who snare or trap animals with leg traps. I read the suggested amendment and I must say that, at least in the French version, one is aware that the wording is so general in nature as to lend itself to abuse where it says that "everyone commits an offence who", and I quote:
(h) uses leg traps to snare or trap any animal...
To my mind, this should be more specific because, in the mind of the hon. member, some animals must be excluded from this provision; I presume he is alluding to animals other than thinking animals. Moreover, I agree that saying that the use of leg traps "to snare or trap any animal" is not specific enough in that of course we must mean animals with legs.
From a practical point of view, it remains that the text of the act could be more specific, though the principle of the bill is worthwhile in that its objective is to fight against cruelty to animals and I congratulate the hon. member for his good intentions. He mentioned a while ago that this subject has already been discussed by one or several committees. I believe that because of the play of parliamentary procedure before adjournment of the session, and because of the attitude of hon. members on the committee, this bill did not come back to the House. That is why the hon. member introduced a new bill on the subject today, that is Bill C-221. If the government of Canada had to choose between humane and inhumane methods of trapping or snaring, needless to say it would opt for the less cruel methods.
Traps are inhumane when they do not kill the animal immediately or when they hold it prisoner and needlessly cause it stress. I agree that the trapping industry would be the first to benefit from a more merciful trapping method. Indeed, the fur of an animal which has struggled is often damaged. If it succeeds in getting free and loses a leg, the animal stays lame

February 14, 1978
Cruelty to Animals
and its fur is lost. However, even though the national conscience and the industry can benefit from more suitable trapping methods, no trap or group of traps can yet be considered truly humane. Among those who want to promote humane trapping methods, some state that by prohibiting leg traps and other inhumane practices, we would inevitably promote the development of an alternative method. They say that only such drastic action can force those responsible to do something. However, we might well wonder what would happen if existing traps were prohibited before alternatives are suggested.
Many trappers, most of them native people, have incomes which put them just above the poverty level. Prohibition of these traps would force these people to give up their hunting income perhaps to draw welfare, or to continue illegally their activities in spite of the threat of prosecution. There are already instances of people who violate the regulations and who cannot be punished, and this causes the law to be ignored. Even if there were only a period of one or two years between the interdiction of those traps and the development, testing, manufacture and distribution of generally acceptable traps, what would become of trappers during this time? And what if this period should be extended? What are the chances that generally accepted traps or series of traps could be developed? Have the efforts made so far been successful?
Even though about 3,000 trapping mechanisms have been patented in the last 125 or 150 years, it is only recently that inventors have considered the humane aspect an important factor in the design of traps. The rewards offered for many years have not always gone to the inventors of humane trapping methods; this is now the case of the award previously of $10,000 and now of $20,000 offered by the American Humane Society since the twenties. However, it must be recognized that there has been very little publicity to make this reward known to those who can design such traps.
Through trap exchange programs, a number of attempts have been made to change the attitude of trappers about new techniques. But these exchanges may have come too soon. For example, a trap tested under this program is still in the development stage some 40 years after it has been designed. We can learn from this experience. The new approved trapping techniques must meet the requirements of the groups that are concerned with the question of humane trapping, because trappers cannot be required to replace their traps several times over. There are now some traps and trapping techniques that are less cruel than others. But no alternative program can be implemented before we reach a definition of what a humane trapping technique is.
In spite of these various difficulties, the federal government has committed itself to finding an alternative. The fact that this government participates in the proceedings of the federal-provincial review committee for humane trapping techniques is a step forward in this direction. This committee was set up in 1973 to promote the development of less cruel techniques and to assess their relative advantages.

More that 160 proposals were sent to the federal-provincial committee, of which the 22 most promising have undergone trials to date. A number of the proposed designs were already on the market under a "humane" label and in popular use. Mechanical tests have been conducted by the Canadian Standards Association and the engineering department of the University of Guelph. The Veterinary College of Ontario also conducted biological tests in Guelph and the provinces proceeded to experiments in the field. Mechanical, biological and practical test data are being assessed for a wide range of factors,including humane and method selectivity features, such as the effects on the animal's fur, easy portability as in a packsack for instance, the safety aspect in respect of both trappers and children and pets in some areas, mechanical durability and cost.
Minimum standards will soon be established on the basis of test results. Those standards will be amended as needed in light of further tests. Always on the lookout for new inventions, the federal-provincial committee issued a brochure on humane trapping for inventors. The Department of Fisheries and Environment is encouraging industry and inventors to co-operate with the government in the search for a solution to the problem of cruel trapping methods.
If a less cruel trap or series of traps is finally uncovered, the next question will be what type of program should be established to replace and take out of use the five million traps or so that would become obsolete in Canada. Should trappers be expected to bear alone the financial burden? The government is concerned with both animals and trappers. The department is therefore committed to support efforts to solve that further problem, trap replacement.
Even if a trap or a series of traps were developed to replace the present types of traps, it would still be necessary to ensure their judicious use. Indeed the most sophisticated traps can still be inhumane if badly used. It is therefore necessary to establish a program to teach the right way to use traps. Even if we do not succeed in finding a ideal way of trapping, the present traps could be made less cruel if the trapper knew how to use them. Acknowledging this fact, the provincial and territorial authorities have developed for the benefit of the trappers, information programs, some of which are partly subsidized by the federal government. The Canadian Trappers Federation is distributing a guide for trappers and resources from the federal government have been used to finance this information campaign.
A training program should help teach unexperienced trappers the art of trapping so that the preys may be killed as quickly as possible, taking into account the limits of the device being used. Professional trappers know how to practise some form of selection of the species, by using specific twigs or baits for instance. Their knowledge should be transmitted to other trappers. The federal government could institute such a training program for trapping carried out on native people land and other federal lands. If the provinces need assistance to increase the scope of their own training programs, the federal govern-
February 14, 1978

ment will put its own specialists at their disposal. The issues of a general nature dealing with the responsibilities related to the implementation of the various aspects of the trapping method humanization program will be studied jointly with the provinces as soon as the standards applicable to humane trapping methods are established.
The government is pleased to see that people calling for the humanization of trapping methods are trying to speed up the development of an improved trap. The federal government strongly hopes that a merciful method of trapping will be found and is allocating resources to efforts made in that respect. It must also ensure that the trapping and fur industries do not have to suffer from modern advancement in this area.
Trapping still has a role to play in this new age but it is no longer limited to fur harvesting. Close to human settlements the trapping of certain species helps prevent eventual conflicts with man. A certain balance between the viable fur animal population and its environment can also be maintained today through the use of traps. This aspect of the management of the ecosystem is certainly profitable while not requiring any expenditures from the government.
It is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that trapping cannot endanger any animal species. The number of trapping permits is determined by the provinces based on the level of optimum population to be maintained in each area. Animal overpopulation leads to the depletion of habitat resources, fights between species, sickness and long term depopulation. That is why the maintenance of a balance between animal populations can be considered a form of humanization in itself because it protects the species against those scourges. Those asking that all forms of trapping be banned should take those factors into consideration in their fight.
Furs are a renewable resource of which Canada can be proud. Those who want to replace furs by synthetic products are de facto advocating the use of petroleum by-products which are non-renewable resources. Just the development of those by-products often destroys habitats which can lead to an irreparable disappearance of wildlife. In concluding, Mr. Speaker, it is essential that we consider all aspects of the issue of humane trapping methods rather than limit ourselves to the one advocated by the supporters of the formal banning of leg-hold traps.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT USE OF ANIMAL STEEL LEG TRAPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the parliamentary secretary reading, quoting and paraphrasing a document published by Fisheries and Environment Canada, dealing with inhumane trapping, "The Desire and The Reality." I would like to quote from a piece of correspondence by The Association for the Protection of FurBearing Animals. The association said on January 31, 1978, that the publication to which we have been exposed is an interesting article that devotes approximately two and a half lines describing its desire to develop humane traps. The remaining six and a half pages seemingly are devoted to justify-
Cruelty to Animals
ing the reasons for not developing humane traps. They think this speaks volumes for itself.
I heartily concur with the position taken by the organization, but I must say in the same breath, Mr. Speaker, that while I am opposed to inhumane traps, and specifically the leg-hold trap, I am not opposed to trapping per se. I should put on record a comment by Dr. N. S. Novakowski, program coordinator of the Canadian Wildlife Service, Department of the Environment. His comment was, and I quote:
Because this topic has been discussed and argued for many decades with little result, we should make every effort to solve it. To ignore it would be to turn our backs on a large body of public opinion.
That statement made by the program co-ordinator of the Canadian Wildlife Service, the federal Department of the Environment, was made in the year 1958.
The real issue surrounding the development of a humane trap can best be summarized by advancing a quote from a letter that I have received from a Mr. Leo Rutledge of Hudson Hope, British Columbia. He says:
It seems highly improbable that a practical killer trap will ever be devised for the wary ones of the dog family. But then one might well ask: is it an absolute essential that we should kill the possible maximum of these? (or of anything else for that matter). To strike a pose as removers of predators and so benefactors to the livestock and poultry industries seems an improbable reason. It lacks credibility. The price of fox and coyote furs has only recently emerged from a 25-year state of depression when relatively few were caught because it did not pay to trap them. Rather that being "alarmed" it is doubtful if the livestock people noticed the difference. At any rate traps, leg-hold or otherwise, would be a doubtful agent of control. The northern canines increase and decrease in their own time. Traps and snares are not an influence of consequence.
Finally, while still discussing Mr. Priest's defence of the leg-hold trap; how apt is the quote from the president of the Canadian Trappers Federation, Mr. L. Cook's report, "You can fool some of the people some of the time but not all of the people all of the time".
The leg-hold trap must be considered the ultimate in barbarism but if the development of a "humane" trap is to mean the total exclusion of pain and frantic anxiety, there can never be one. At best there can be only those less inhumane.
No trap can ever be the answer to all needs because the constraints and variables contingent are infinite. So be it. Let us then proceed with what we have now devised and that which we know can be done.
There have been killer traps available for many years capable of practical use on animals up to the size of the fisher, and these in the bigger sizes may also be used successfully on some of the larger animals such as beaver and wolverine. Wolves, being now classed as big game, need not be considered. In other words we have nearly all the essentials now-and perhaps all we are likely to get. So there is really little to wait for.
The higher price of one of the better known killer traps has been one of the averred objections to conversion. An argument of some validity, perhaps, while fur prices were resting in the doldrums, but with some of the fur bearers trading at $100 and occasionally even better, the cost-benefit ratio is now entirely different.
Price, weight, bulk, dependability, ease of setting and ability to kill are among the factors to be considered in devising a "humane" trap. Strangely enough, none of these were problems to the deadfall of yesteryear. Perhaps it would be well to take a second look here lest it should hold a partial solution. Improved trigger assemblies of various sizes and perfect in design could now be mass produced for pennies; with the aid of the small modern power saw the woodwork would be simple. Some trappers may have spare time in the summer. If so, it could be done then and building a thousand deadfalls should not seem an unreasonable objective. No special skills are required and once built they would remain serviceable for years.

February 14, 1978
Cruelty to Animals
The government funds made available to various aspiring "humane" trap builders have been rather well publicized. Therefore, results, per dollar expended, may well prove to be politically rewarding but other yields are likely to be unimpressive. All too often and easily, our leaders, our decision-makers, tend to defer the decision to further study, more research, the consultant's consultant, the committees, the subcommittees and all the other devices to stall for time, the more opportune political climate, the diffusing of responsibility, the guise of something productive being done, the "peace in my time" and ultimately the dead end. In the real world it is called "passing the buck".
The article "They take so long to die" sees the present government funding for the development of a "humane" trap "as only a scratch on the surface" because someone has estimated that it will require $150,000 per year "To get the job done". The estimate did not include how many "per annums" were deemed essential. How these conclusions were arrived at will forever remain a mystery to me. Really! Estimators should be more careful lest they trigger something-like a rash of government grants. In my opinion, $150,000 per annum or any other additional "humane" trap funding can only serve to buy a bigger pile of procrastinations. If legislators will now proceed to enact in a decisive manner, the marketplace will react and builders of better traps will beat a path to our door.
I suggest there is sufficient evidence at hand to act and that legislators should now do so. The facts are in and the time has come. The leg-hold trap-useful to our survival in its time-has served its purpose. It can no longer possibly be held as acceptable to the mores of our contemporary society. It has become an anomaly to our way of life. It is out of step. Already it is very late. The leg-hold trap has been able to outstay its time only because it operated in relative obscurity. Most were used well removed from the mainstream of society.
But though the leg-hold trap has become foreign to our culture, we should not be unduly harsh and speak of it despairingly. It served us well as a useful and dependable tool in our time of need. Instead, let us now take it to the museum with some decorum and place it with our other many and varied anachronisms- the thumbscrew, the wheel, the rack and the garrotte. The end is inevitable. So let us now acquiesce-sooner rather than later-while we can still do so with some grace.
I am quite aware that new rules and implicit compliance are not one and the same thing. There may well be some leg-hold traps in use two decades after being outlawed. All the more reason for an immediate start. We must act if legislators are to react and so ultimately enact. If we, as a people, do not express disapproval we thereby imply approval. We condone. There is no room for fence riding here. By a land stand of no dissent, we in fact give tacit consent.
British Columbia's attitudes to the raw-fur resources have been traditionally progressive. 1925-26 saw trapping areas of defined borders established throughout the province. These borders were recognized by the "Game Department" and their contained areas became known as registered trap lines. This system was the first of its kind and intelligent resource utilization was thereby ensured in lieu of former haphazard exploitation. This was a major breakthrough and undoubtedly among the most enlightened wildlife legislation ever enacted in Canada. It would now be fitting if B.C. again led wildlife legislation in an enlightened way by relegating the leg-hold trap to the past. Young people in search of causes to champion need look no further than this. And they could slay this dragon overnight if they choose to do so.
Finally, as a point of information-and lest it be thought that I might be little, old and wearing tennis shoes-I have spent 42 years in northern B.C. as a big game guide and outfitter. For 15 of the earliest years I also ran a 13-cabin trap line and made thousands of sets with leg-hold traps. I entered the north when options were few and easily defined. If one did not wish to leave he could stay and hunt or stay and starve. I elected to stay, hunt and live. The economy was fur. Trappers were either good hunters or they were not. The criterion of "good" was ability to consistently return with a sizeable catch of fur. Hunters, whether two or four-legged, hunted to live and the method was not a consideration of the time.
Leo Rutledge
Hudson Hope, B.C.
When Mr. Rutledge talks about a deadline it should be noted that his letter is dated March 25, 1974. Since that time the committee on humane trapping has appeared before the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry and has made a report of a buck-passing nature. The Department of Fisher-

ies and the Environment has, it is true, produced a pamphlet on the subject and the "motherhood statements" contained within that literary exercise are truly amazing. The suggestion that the federal government should teach trappers how to trap shows a total lack of understanding of trapping and trappers. The suggestion that the federal government might control the Crown land in which the trappers operate and constrain them in some fashion other than the way in which it is done in British Columbia is another indication that the government would like to impinge upon men who are probably the freest spirits in Canada's north.
In many instances trappers are concerned about the inhumanity of existing leg-hold traps. Experienced trappers are more equipped for obtaining their furs with little damage and with more humanity than inexperienced or novice trappers. That does not remove from us, the trapping industry or the trapper the responsibility of resolving this problem. This problem has been in existence as long as the leg-hold trap has been in use.
I support the private member's bill of the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon). I am sure many trappers in my constituency will realize that I do not want to deny them an opportunity to earn a livelihood. The federal-provincial committee has one of the best boondoggles going for it: a budget of several hundreds of thousands of dollars, as well as an opportunity to delay decisions. This nonsense has been going on for years. If I was lazy, I would want to be associated with that committee. I do not wish to wallow in the public trough in that fashion, or in any fashion for that matter.
I conclude by indicating that I support the private member's bill before the House today.

speechtext:
If the hon. member opposite would listen for a moment, he would realize that I excluded him. I do not suppose listening is one of his characteristics.
The hon. member used up a lot of time explaining his position. I will attempt to make my comments in as few words as possible. Many of those people who express concern seem to
February 14, 1978

come from urban areas. They wear leather shoes, and there are other differences. When one refers to trapping, obviously an animal is going to be killed. Fur-bearing animals are killed in order to adorn people. There are few furs which are needed for real purposes. Basically they are used to make people more attractive in the eyes of someone else.
There seems to be a contradiction in this entire area, as well as some hypocrisy. People who live in urban areas often wear fur trim themselves, as well as leather shoes. They have views about how other people in different parts of Canada are living. In this case, they have views about trappers who are using the leg trap and are promoting a more humane method of trapping. There is no question that everyone wants more humane trapping. The question seems to be: is there a more humane and practical form of trapping which is readily available?
Various brochures have been published, such as the one on humane trap development and the one a la recherche du progres, referring to testing systems for humane traps. There is some contradiction in the opinions of people who are knowledgeable in this area. But then I have always found a contradiction in the definition of the term "humane killing". No one can kill something humanely. 1 realize people are omnivorous and eat meat, but most of them would find it offensive to spend an afternoon in an abattoir, especially those who are not accustomed to it. I am from the city of Toronto, but on occasion I have had to butcher animals when I was living in the country. I have lived in areas where it was necessary to butcher goats and sheep, and I have never found that process to be attractive. It is necessary to slit the goat's throat. How can that be done humanely? Either you do it or you don't.
In preparation for rising today, I had occasion to look at that section of the Criminal Code dealing with cruelty in trapping and cruelty to animals. It seems to me that it would be more important to argue against killing animals rather than working toward arriving at a more humane trapping method. I argue strongly in favour of not killing fur-bearing animals for decorative purposes, rather than arguing in favour of killing fur-bearing animals for decorative purposes in a more humane manner.
Somehow the logic of this argument escapes me. I have had occasion to visit northern Canada as well as other parts of the world. The hon. member for Kootenay West talked about wolves and other animals. There are places in the tropical world where people kill everything that moves, and the furs are sold to Canada where coats are made. Ocelots and other exotic animals are killed for this purpose. An hon. member pointed out that snakes are also killed for their skins. The crocodile population is being wiped out. The skins of some of these animals are used only to hold up somebody's trousers. Alligator skins are used to make extremely expensive shoes for very wealthy people.

It seems somewhat beside the point to discuss whether animals are killed humanely. Mr. Speaker, when five o'clock was called 1 was referring to a letter 1 had received from the town of Haines Junction in the Yukon and putting on the record the problems they are encountering in trying to obtain land not only for government purposes but for the purpose of building a trailer court and other things. I should like to read the following three paragraphs of the letter:
The Alaska Highway paving program (Shakwak Project), a ten-year program, is scheduled to begin in June this year, with between 80-100 employees in our community. The Alcan pipeline route is also scheduled to pass within a few miles of our community, our portion is presently scheduled for 1981. How can

this community even begin to have a hope of accommodating the impact of these projects when land is not being made available for development by people, nor is land being made available for utilities such as water, sewer, larger lagoons etc. If some action is not taken immediately the results can only be tragic.
They say they have written to the present minister and to former ministers on numerous occasions. They are faced with an influx of people but cannot get land on which to build the necessary housing or trailer court to accommodate them. This shows a complete lack of understanding on the part of the federal government and indicates the need for the people of the Yukon to have an opportunity of determining their destiny.
Another matter that I should like to touch on briefly with respect to the pipeline is the question of Canadian equity. This is a subject which was mentioned yesterday by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen). The pipeline project is one of the largest in Canadian history. It will require large amounts of capital, something in the neighbourhood of $4.5 billion to $5 billion, which will come from Canadian and United States markets.
If one examines the history of Alberta Gas Trunk Line, one of the partners in the Foothills project, it will be noted that when AGTL was set up Alberta residents were given the first option to purchase shares in the company. They acquired an equity that over the years has been an excellent investment due to the appreciation in the shares and the dividends that accrued.
If an arrangement were worked out in the present instance whereby Canadians could purchase equity shares, it would mean that less money would have to be borrowed on the foreign market, at substantial savings in interest to the people of Canada. We speak of foreign investment in our country and the outflow of Canadian capital to the United States and other countries. What better way to keep capital at home than to allow Canadians to purchase equity shares in the Foothills pipeline?
I should like to make one further recommendation, Mr. Speaker, and I must emphasize that I am expressing a personal opinion and not necessarily the policy of this party. Why not arrange for Canadians to purchase equity shares in the company and, to encourage such an investment, amend the Income Tax Act to provide for the waiver of capital gains tax in cases where the shares purchased are held for a period of two years or more, or, alternatively, allow the amount of the purchase price of these shares to be an exemption for income tax purposes? Canadian equity investment is vital. This party will insist that the government allow the widest possible participation by Canadians in the pipeline financing.

In closing, 1 would like to say that concern about the environment, the effect of a pipeline on the ecology, and the socioeconomic problems that exist, has been expressed by Berger, Lysyk, and numerous individuals and organizations who have appeared before various bodies which were holding hearings. All of these questions are important and must be
February 14, 1978

looked at in perspective. The Yukon has faced many of these problems before and has had experience dealing with them. There is a population of 24,000 in the Yukon but each summer there is an influx of some 350,000 visitors. Foothills advise that at its peak construction period the maximum number of employees who will be working in the Yukon will be 2,200. If you add to that their families, the maximum number of people who will be resident in the Yukon specifically with respect to the pipeline will be some 5,000 people
The Yukon has seen the construction of the Alaska Highway built with guts and tractors by the U.S. Army Corps, of Engineers. The work was begun in March 1942 and completed in nine months. In the early 1940s it saw the construction of the Canol pipeline, involving 1,600 miles of pipe and 1,000 miles of road. This cost $137 million and took 20 months to complete, excavating beneath the permafrost through the Mackenzie mountains while at times temperatures fell to 70 degrees below zero. The construction of the Haines-Fairbanks pipeline took place in 1954-55. It was 620 miles long, with 292 miles in Canada, and carried 12,000 barrels a day. There are other projects as well. I mention these few examples to indicate that in the Yukon the residents and local authorities are able to cope with fairly substantial projects. These projects have had minimal impact and the area remains a relatively beautiful and virgin territory. The people in the Yukon are able to adapt.
My plea through you, Mr. Speaker, to the government is to give to the people of the Yukon, through their elected representatives, the power and responsibility to deal with and solve problems that arise as a result of the pipeline construction. Let us not see a massive influx of federal civil servants involving themselves in problems that can be dealt with by the people who are native to or who have lived in the north for many years, and who have the ability to understand and solve the problems associated with pipeline construction and development of the north.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to take part in what I consider this most important debate on Bill C-25, but it is with some concern that I see the government forging ahead with the debate on this bill before the National Energy Board has published the contents of its report. As we have always demonstrated, the energy matter is always a matter of big money, without regard for the environmental and socioeconomic aspects which we must learn to appreciate, as soon as possible, for our own survival. Had it not been for the foresight, the objectivity, and the rigor manifested by Justice Berger during his three-year inquiry on the environmental and socioeconomic effects of the Mackenzie Valley pipeline construction, once again, as a nation, we would have infringed on the individual freedom of natives, and caused irreparable damage on an extremely delicate environment to which we are total strangers.
The recommendations made by Justice Berger take into consideration the opinions put forth by the two main groups
Northern Pipeline
who fought this project, namely the Canadian Arctic Resources Committee and the Committee on Justice and Freedom. The former categorically requested abandonment of the project, while the latter argued for a ten-year moratorium on the entire question of northern development.
As we know, the commission of inquiry chaired by Justice Thomas R. Berger was set up in March 1974 as a result of the enormous difficulties, financial, technical and social, created by the project in which two companies, namely Arctic Gas and Foothills Pipeline, had already invested considerable amounts of money. Contrary to what usually happens, the commission took an active part in the debate during the meetings through advisors who repeatedly stressed that the applicants, that is the companies, were in a position to prove their claims, particularly where engineering and construction were concerned. For instance, the commission produced the theorical testimony of Dr. P. Williams of Carleton University in Ottawa according to which the underground pipeline of the Arctic Gas would be subject to differential upheavals that could damage it seriously, and technical methods to reduce or avoid such continuous uplift of the buried and refrigerated pipeline were still in their infancy. To our mind, that was a weighty argument in favour of putting off the project to a later date.
From the social point of view, the methods used by Justice Berger to collect the testimony of the indigenous populations was also remarkable since, far from limiting himself to those of the inhabitants of big cities, the centres of economic and political power such as Yellowknife, Inuvik and Fort Smith, he went to the trouble of travelling 1,700 miles throughout the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, using all means of transport including the canoe and the dog sled, to listen to 1,317 witnesses in 300 days of public hearings and give an opportunity to the native Denes and Inuit who represent most of the inhabitants of the towns and villages to state their opinion while the members of the commission paid close attention to them as if they were experts.
The position of the natives on the pipeline is well summarized in a few words found on page 11 of the lengthy Berger report. It will cross lands that are claimed by Canada's native people, a region where the struggle for a new social and economic order and political responsibility is taking place.
Canadians remember that unhealthy incapacity of the federal government to remain unbiased in its decisions about the development of energy resources, an incapacity which we pointed out on several occasions and which is due to the fact that it is entirely dependent on oil companies for its information. Regarding this, Justice Berger was very critical in his report of government industry co-operative efforts. Although it is neither realistic nor financially feasible to duplicate all industry services, there is a solution to that basic problem. According to Mr. Lewis Auerbach, scientific advisor to the Science Council of Canada, it would be possible to selectively reproduce key data for the evaluation of projects put forward by the federal government.

February 14, 1978
Northern Pipeline
There again, the Trudeau government cannot say it is not aware of such possibilities, because the council with which Mr. Auerbach is working is directly subsidized by the federal government. In his conclusions, Justice Berger paid no heed to Canadian economic needs for Mackenzie Delta gas. In order to show another facet, we now refer to an economic study of the Arctic pipeline which takes no account of environment, social nor other ramifications for the north and its inhabitants. That study by Mr. John F. Helliwell of the Economics Department of B.C. University was tabled with the National Energy Board and is reported on in the summer 1977 edition of the Journal Analyses de Politiques.
Concerning the over-all effect of an Arctic pipeline on the national economy, Mr. Helliwell feels that barring fortuitous circumstances, there is no assurance the implementation of such a project will help stabilize economic growth. But in the same breath he adds that such a project, however big, can be implemented if the public and private sectors give it top priority and agree to slacken the demand for other resources, which confirms our view that the money and human resources needed for such projects are so huge it is impossible to develop at the same time other energy sources, including renewable sources. This therefore inevitably leads to an energy impasse.
According to our economist, cost estimates submitted by the applicants are grossly understated, in an attempt to prove the project is viable, in the face of small proven reserves in the Mackenzie Delta. He feels real costs were 125 per cent higher than stated by the oil companies, a type of evaluation error responsible for the fact that a project such as the Trans-Alaska pipeline, that was to cost Canadians $2 million per mile before 1970, will in fact cost the taxpayer $10 million per mile, with unforeseen overspending accumulating day after day. As opposed to the 8.5 per cent annual growth forecast made in 1975 by the National Energy Board for natural gas demand, the Helliwell study covering the period from 1974 to 1980 puts the estimated annual growth at 3 per cent.
From 1974 to 1976, actual demand increased only by 2 per cent and not by 8.5 per cent. We must therefore seriously question the intentions of the National Energy Board in this regard. The board is very conservative as concerns gas supplies, and this attitude also prevails among the applying companies which, according to Helliwell, are "pessimistic in their estimates of potential supplies and take no account whatsoever of supplies located in areas of the country other than frontier areas, even though all parties recognize that there are proven reserves in these areas".
When we look at gas supplies estimates, we note that the shortage expected will occur only in the mid-nineties. We are therefore wery far from the figures quoted by the applying companies which predict that by 1985 we shall have a deficit equivalent to one million barrels of oil a day. Because of all these factors, and always according to Helliwell, Canada would be wise to postpone construction of a pipeline in this area of the country. Helliwell also adds that it is not at all obvious that the Alcan route, which is the route recently approved by the National Energy Board for the construction of

a pipeline, will avoid the problems caused in the case of the Mackenzie Delta project, and this from an economic viewpoint, even though this route seems to have the advantage of avoiding any trouble with native land claims and of being less damaging to the environment. What greatly concerns the economist is the pressure exerted by the urgent needs of the United States on Canada's decision, which pressure could impose on us costs which do not justify the expected benefits.
We, of the Social Credit Party of Canada, believe that the government should see to it that the Americans do not reap all the benefits of this endeavour and let us support the consequences of all the environmental damages. The government should negotiate with the natives with all due consideration to their rights as native owners of the territories concerned. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am very happy to have the opportunity to participate in this historic debate on the northern pipeline, Bill C-25. It will authorize and make provision to regulate the northern Alcan pipeline which will provide a land bridge or source of transportation for gas from the Alaskan-Prudhoe Bay fields to the lower 48 states and, at the same time, make provision for a connection for the delta and Beaufort Sea gas to be transported to southern Canada at a later stage.
This pipeline is historic in many ways. I do not believe there has ever been an engineering project that has received so much attention, so much planning and so much construction engineering as this one since the discovery of gas and oil in Prudhoe Bay in 1968. Perhaps no project has had so much money spent on it as well in terms of study. The Arctic gas company spent something like $140 million just to lose the nod of approval to Alcan.
Perhaps no project has received more study through royal commissions and environmental impact statements than this project which, of course, was the subject of the Lysyk and Berger inquiries as well as hearings by the environmental assessment panel of the federal government. Perhaps no project, at least in the history of Canada, has received more study by such a great number of governments, including the territorial governments of the Yukon and Northwest Territories, the several provincial governments concerned, as well as the federal government, and, on the United States side, the government of Alaska and the U.S. federal government. Surely the National Energy Board hearings that were held were among the most lengthy ever. I believe the length of the project, over 5,000 miles of large diameter pipe, is a first. So by all measurements this is one of the largest projects in the history of Canada or any other country.
Perhaps the largest aspect of it is the financial dimension of the project, now estimated at $10 billion. To put that in perspective, that is about 20 times the cost of the St. Lawrence Seaway when it was constructed in 1952.
This project, in the early years at least, will be designed to transport gas to the lower 48 states from the Prudhoe Bay fields. From Canada's point of view it becomes an important project in terms of providing economic activity in our country and a service to our U.S. neighbours; Alcan estimates some
February 14, 1978

$400 million to $500 million in services per year to transport that gas across Canadian territory.
Surely at this time when we see projects of this magnitude costing, in this case, $10 billion, and when more projects are on the drawing boards for nuclear plants, for oil and gas exploration, for uranium mine development and for coal development costing hundreds of millions of dollars-literally billions-this should make us more conscious of the need for energy conservation.
It is nice to know that this aspect is going forward as well in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. Last week I met two young people who will be working in my constituency at conservation community clinics. They had attended the conservation office of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources in Ottawa taking the intensive training program. 1 must say they were very enthusiastic and very determined that they were going to make a real contribution toward the Canadian and world energy crisis. Although this is not spectacular-unlike the spending of $10 billion for this northern pipeline-surely it is terribly important that we learn conservation as well, because the habits developed now are ones that will last forever and do not represent a one-time expenditure.
If we have to make expenditures of this magnitude for energy projects in this country, even though it is for our U.S. neighbours initially, now is a good time to be doing it. We are going through a period in the next two years when we will have a very large number of people coming into the labour force in this country. Toward the 1980s that will taper off and the number of people coming into the labour force will be reduced. Therefore, during the next few years we should be taking on and carrying out these massive national projects which will provide employment, capital investment and economic activity in our country, resulting in a long-term benefit as well.
Certainly the economic benefits to our country of this project are very significant. The Foothills company projects that 90 per cent of this project on the Canadian leg will be spent on the cost of services in Canada. This means that at the escalated price of $3.3 billion, some $3 billion will be spent in Canada for Canadian work. Some 68,000 man-years of work will be created over the five to seven-year period of construction. If we take into account the total Dempster link as well, as the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) has estimated we are talking in terms of 100,000 jobs. If we look at just the manufacturing aspect of this construction project, we envisage some 30,000 jobs alone being created.
The company estimates that one-half of one per cent of the gross national product will come from this project during the period 1979 to 1981. During the period from 1977 to 2005, it is estimated that $500 million per year will accrue to Canada in terms of balance of payments benefits. Also the company has estimated that during this 28-year period approximately $13.6 billion of benefit will flow from the United States to Canada. The purchase of pipe alone will involve over one million tons of pipe costing $1.2 billion. The 30 compressors
Northern Pipeline
required can be produced in Canada. They will cost $158 million, according to the company's estimate. Thus, the economic benefits are significant.
In terms of jobs to the Yukon, it has been estimated that there will be 2,200 jobs during the peak period, and approximately $177 million will be spent in that territory. In the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia, approximately $1.6 billion will be spent. In Ontario and Quebec some $1.2 billion will be spent. The economic benefit is not just in the west but is spread right accross Canada. It will help communities like Hamilton and Welland. Surely the benefits will spill over to a company like Algoma Steel in Sault Ste. Marie, which is located partially in my constituency. In terms of construction, approximately 7,800 jobs will be created on the project at its peak.
The government and the bill commit this project to having a maximum of Canadian content. The objectives of the bill spell this out very well. The minister, through his powers of approving the procurement program of the company, ensures there will be a maximum amount of Canadian content. At the same time, it is in Canada's interest to have competitive bidding so that the project can be carried out within the estimated cost. If the project is constructed within 135 per cent of the estimated cost, that means American consumers of gas will be responsible for paying the transportation of gas between Dawson Creek and Whitehorse, which is a distance of approximately 277 miles, for the entire history of the operation of the Dempster link. Canadian steelmakers have welcomed the competitive bidding arrangement. They are not concerned about competing with American companies. Indeed, they have projected that they will bid successfully on some of the pipe in the United States and Alaskan sector as well. Regularly our steel industry bids and competes successfully against United States companies.
Surely the final decision as to the size of the pipe for the Canadian section of the pipeline must rest with Canada. The consultations which are ongoing with the United States now are necessary. We must make provision for the size of pipe which will carry gas from the Mackenzie Delta to southern Canada. Provision for adequate capacity must be made. Since Interprovincial Steel and Pipe Corporation, Ltd. and the Steel Company of Canada, Ltd. are able to meet the requirement for low pressure pipe, surely the ultimate decision of the National Energy Board and the government must be to choose a pipe which can be manufactured in Canada. When Ipsco has completed its $80 million expansion program in P.egina, it will be able to provide approximately one-third of the required pipe, and Stelco has the capacity to provide approximately two-thirds. The naturally desirable arrangement would be for these companies to provide the pipe.
Initially the pipe will transport American gas to American consumers. At a later stage when the Dempster link is connected and the sources of supply in the delta and Beaufort are tapped, the pipeline will supply gas to southern Canada. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, when that link is connected, it will provide approximately 10 per cent of the gas supplied to the
2862

Canadian market. Surely at that time it will be more vital to Canada than to the United States.
In the short term, the economic benefit to Canada will be the provision of jobs. The bill makes it clear that there will be a great deal of benefit provided to the Yukon. The people in that territory will be given the first opportunity for work and the provision of supplies. The company has indicated that it will provide a gas supply to the major communities of the Yukon. One report indicated that this will save the average household $200 per year; that is, through the use of natural gas rather than oil to heat their houses.
In his negotiations with the United States, the minister has been able to make a very favourable arrangement in terms of providing a $200 million advance payment to the Yukon to cover the socioeconomic costs there, as well as to provide for advance tax payments up to 1981 of some $35 million, and beyond that, payments of $30 million per year. Over the 25-year projected life of the project, that will amount to approximately $1 billion of benefits to the Yukon Territory, which surely is a significant gain.
The central aspect of this bill is to provide a northern pipeline agency, a single window agency, to regulate and control all aspects of the development of the pipeline. This is a good idea. It will provide for the delegation of authority from the National Energy Board, the Department of Fisheries and the Environment, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. It will provide for consultation with the provincial and territorial governments as well. This agency will be concerned with the physical aspects of the pipe, as well as the native questions, the social and environmental aspects and Canadian content. It will be a situation where one administrator will report to a commissioner, and ultimately to the minister in Ottawa. Surely the socioeconomic and native questions will be of as much concern to that agency as the physical aspects of the pipeline.
One question which the committee will want to study will be the relationship between the designated minister and the minister responsible for the National Energy Board, if they do not happen to be the same minister, because ultimately the responsibility for this pipeline will revert to the NEB. 1 think that interplay between the two ministers will be an important aspect which we will want to have clarified in the committee.
The idea of a single agency is a very good one because in 1975 the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works did a very extensive study on oil and gas supplies from frontier regions and on transportation systems. During the course of that study we went to Alaska and met with senior officials who were carrying out the construction of the Alyeska pipeline. That was just at the period of time when the Alyeska pipeline was about two-thirds complete. They described the mechanism under which they were working. Authority from the various agencies of the federal government and the various agencies and departments of the state department was delegat-

ed. There was one person at ground level where the decision to proceed with construction was made. The senior people with whom we met said that without this delegated authority to a person actually on the ground the pipeline would never have been completed. It would have bogged down in red tape.
The establishment of this kind of central agency is a very good idea which will ensure that this kind of authority is delegated to people actually on the construction site, so that the project can move forward, be completed on time and not be bogged down and held up.
Another important aspect which is provided for in the bill is consultation and agreement with the provinces and territorial governments. Many of the provincial governments, like Alberta, have extensive expertise in regulating and controlling pipelines, so it is natural that the federal government will want to have a liaison with those groups and take advantage of their expertise. A formalized structure is laid out in the bill for a consultative mechanism. Consultation every three months would not be a very practical arrangement, although it might be good for long-term discussions.
It seems to me that the direct consultation with the minister which is provided for would be beneficial. However, surely consultation with the territorial governments will be even more important, especially with the Yukon in the initial stages, but also with the Northwest Territories when the Dempster link is dealt with, because proportionately this will a very much larger project to the Yukon than it will be to the provincial governments involved. I met with several councillors and assemblymen in the Yukon in early December. 1 had a chance to discuss this, and they were very concerned that there might not be adequate consultation and that they might not have an active part in the discussion and development of this pipeline.
Likewise, when the Dempster link is established there should be a very good liaison and consultation process with the Northwest Territories Council. One councillor told me recently that a resolution was passed in October proposing an alternative to the Dempster link, the Canol line. Under the proposal the line would run from Johnson's Crossing on the Alaska Highway to Norman Wells, along the Mackenzie River and to the delta reserves. I am not sure of the details of that proposal, but if there is adequate consultation with the Northwest Territories Council, there will be an opportunity for the proposal to be fully explored.
Another aspect of the bill which I think is very important and very good is that the cost of the agency will be borne by the Foothills company. This will ensure that there will be constant pressure on the company to complete the line on time, and that they do everything in their power to avoid strikes and delays. The company will not only bear the financial cost of delays, but will also bear the cost of the regulatory agency if the project is held up because of the company's lack of foresight or organization.
In conclusion, it seems to me that the northern pipeline bill is a reasonably good piece of legislation with which to develop this northern project. It is designed to ensure that the pipeline is built efficiently through the use of a single window agency.

The bill will ensure the maximum number of jobs for Canadians, that environmental precautions are taken, that the social needs of the people of the north are met and that precautions are taken to ensure the financial integrity of the project. It will provide a good consultation mechanism and provide for agreements with the various provincial and territorial governments.
I hope the bill will not be unduly delayed by debate in the House, that the project can be discussed in the special committee and the beneficial economic effects of the bill are passed on to all Canadians at a time when they are very greatly needed.

Any self-respecting parliament that would pass this bill with its present provisions and pass the whole thing over to the executive branch should be arrested for criminal negligence. This bill provides for nothing except an annual report to be filed in parliament. Clause 13 provides for an annual report to be filed, but it does not say what should be in the report, just that the agency shall prepare a report relating to its operations and that the minister will cause it to be tabled in parliament.
If the legislation is passed as it stands, all we can get in the future is an annual report. We do not even dictate what is to be in the report. We do not even say that the objectives for Canadian content and how that is being realized shall be in the report or anything about the financial arrangements.
I know that the official opposition will be putting forward amendments to correct that when we reach committee stage, so that the agency will have to report at least quarterly on specific matters. If that provision is not included I am sure no legislator here will accept the bill. If there are no substantive amendments then parliament gives up all its rights in connection with this huge project.

If I were the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources I would not put up with something in my bailiwick being given to another minister-the land grabber, the pipeline grabber, the Deputy Prime Minister. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is responsible for all oil, gas and energy development, but when the biggest project is snatched from him and

Then the report says that the Canadian content actually achieved can vary substantially from estimates because of competitive pricing conditions, tied and concessional financing, government monitoring, corporate attitudes, and other factors. We did not hear that from the government.
Then it has tables which show that the best we can expect in Canadian manufacturing content is 81.3 per cent. Table 12 shows estimates of Canadian content. There is a percentage of total expenditures for the construction of Alcan-Dempster; it is 81.3 per cent Canadian. Not 90 per cent, not 85 per cent, not 88 per cent, not 84 per cent, not 82 per cent, but 81.3 per cent. We go on through the table and the figure is $2,299 million. If we add on the construction side of the table, there is a total of $3,367 million Canadian out of $3,940 million which is 85.4 per cent. That is the maximum, and that is if everything goes perfectly; and everything is administered to the utmost perfection. So is the most we can have is 85 per cent with absolute perfection.
What does the Deputy Prime Minister tell us in his speech of yesterday at page 2790 of Hansard? He said this:
During the hearings before the National Energy Board, Foothills stated its objective-and I stress the word objective because it was not and could not be a flat guarantee-
Northern Pipeline
The Deputy Prime Minister is cagey; he is the cagiest cage in the government. He goes on:
-was to achieve Canadian input into the system in Canada of more than 90 per cent.
We have been warned it is only an objective. You cannot catch the Deputy Prime Minister when he says that. Then he goes on to say:
During the intervening months Foothills has repeatedly restated that objective. On the basis of past performance of the sponsoring companies, and our own assessment of Canadian supply capabilities, there is every reason to believe that this target will be achieved.
The Deputy Prime Minister went a bit further than he thought he was going when he said that there is every reason to believe that we can achieve over 90 per cent. Because the report of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce states the most we can achieve is 85 per cent-if we are perfect. God knows this is not a perfect government. We have to be harsh and say there are a few imperfections here. The Deputy Prime Minister is not properly briefed. He is saying we can achieve 90 per cent, but the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, headed by our late comrade, has said the best that can be done is 85 per cent. Our manufacturers will achieve only 82 per cent.
I hope, therefore, that the Deputy Prime Minister will retract his statement at the first opportunity, that he will come before this House is sackcloth and ashes to retract that statement. The government is so secretive. It is governed by stealth and secrecy. It is government by the unknowing doing the unknowable. They do not know what reports they have prepared. Some ministers are in the federal-provincial conference and some are here. They give this "boffle" to the House. It is government in the dark. It reminds me of the old Cole Porter tune "Dancing in the dark". I hope that when government members have their little drinking session here they will sing "Government in the Dark".

speechtext:
We are hearing a lot about GATT. The Deputy Prime Minister said today that we could not put anything in the agreement about Canadian preference, that this would violate GATT. Are the Americans worrying about GATT? It is "rat-a-tat-tat" to GATT. The Americans legislate a "buy-American" policy, which means a complete surrender of Canadian interests.
The industry, trade and commerce report says that if we word it carefully we would have no problem with GATT. But this will not solve the project engineering services that are not affected by GATT. Japan, Germany and the United States don't care about GATT. The only ones who care about GATT are those in this "GATT government". The Canadian people have to get this GATT government so that it will not get them.
We all know Foothills propose a 48-inch pipe, half-inch thick, 1,260 p.s.i. That is fine for Canada. There is a 48-inch pipe, three-quarters of an inch thick, 1,680 p.s.i., which Ipsco cannot make, but which the Americans want because they can make it. We know there is a 54-inch pipe, one half-inch thick, 1,160 psi, which the Americans cannot make but the Canadians can, Ipsco in Regina and Edmonton and Stelco in Welland and Camrose.
Should there be one second, one week, one month or any time taken to make a decision? I do not give a hoot what the

NDP recommended. It is the 54-inch pipe that only Canadians can make which is the pipe we want. If there is some technical reason 1,260 p.s.i. pipe is unsatisfactory, there is the 48-inch pipe that Foothills recommended in the first place.
When it comes to the pipe which is important to Canada, what do we find? If this was not Canada, I would not believe it. If Stelco makes its pipe in Welland, in order to be competitive it has to transport it through the Panama Canal to get to the site of the pipeline. It would be too expensive to transport it by rail. It is unbelievable, but I am told that Foothills are actually having a study done to see what is the best way to transport pipe and other materials.
This country has a railway, but we cannot ship the pipe by rail cheaper from Welland to the Yukon and Alberta. We have to send it through the Seaway, down the seaboard, through the Panama Canal, up the west coast and then by truck or rail. No wonder the British Columbia members are going berserk about the wide flange steel. I would be a "flangist" myself. In fact, I am. We are in the same position in Newfoundland. The freight rates are such that it is cheaper to get steel from Japan rather than central Canada. What a crazy country! We talk about DREE. That is one of the problems.
If the American plant in Texas is going to be able to compete and the cheapest way of getting the materials there is through the Panama Canal, that will be cheaper than shipping from Ontario. According to my atlas, it would be cheaper to ship from Texas. They will have the advantage. Any government that permits that to be done should be strung out and strung up. They should not be permitted to exist. They should change the freight rates or do something to reverse the situation. I just draw the attention of the House to this anomaly.
What is apparently being considered is to use B.C. pulp and lumber carriers which now go east through the canal to the eastern seaboard and return empty. They are to return west filled with steel. That is the proposal being looked at. The United States steel plant is at Baytown, Texas. That is certainly closer to the Yukon if the Panama Canal must be used. That is certainly a strange kettle of fish, as we say in Newfoundland.
There is no reason why we ought to be having a debate in Canada as to whether we should use Canadian steel. It is ludicrous. No other country in the world would have such a debate. There would not be such a debate in Japan, Germany or the United States. Are they raging with debate in the U.S. as to whether they are going to allow foreigners to build their pipeline, supply the pipe and all the rest? They are not. The debate they are having is whether they are going to grab ours. We are wondering whether we are going to save a little bit for ourselves. What kind of a country is this? I would sooner go down fighting than put up with that kind of humiliation.

February 14, 1978

this the Canadian content can only be 50 per cent. I presume there are technical reasons for that.
There are a lot of items apart from the pipe that can and should be Canadian right to the limit, as set out in table 12 of this report which we have not got. We are not supposed to have it because we are not supposed to know anything about this project.
There is another piece of hypocrisy that had slipped my mind. I refer to clause 3(f) on page 3 of the bill. One of the objects of this act is, and I quote:
-to advance national economic and energy interests and to maximize related industrial benefits by ensuring the highest possible degree of Canadian participation in all aspects of the planning and construction of, and procurement for, the pipeline while ensuring that the procurement of goods and services for the pipeline will be on generally competitive terms.
That is stated to be an objective. The rest of the bill contradicts the objectives. It kisses the Americans' you know what in practically every clause.lt is given up altogether when we get to section 7 of the agreement, which is annexed to this bill, dealing with supply of goods and services. I quote:
Having regard to the objectives of this agreement, each government will endeavour to ensure that the supply of goods and services to the pipeline project will be on generally competitive terms. Elements to be taken in to account in weighing competitiveness will include price, reliability, servicing capacity and delivery schedules.
Each government is going to give the other a preference. Each may, and I quote:
-institute consultations with the other in particular cases where it may appear that the objectives of subparagraph (a) are not being met.
This is contradictory to the objective in clause 3(f).
Remedies to be considered would include the renegotiation of contracts or the reopening of bids.
You can bet your bottom dollar, Mr. Speaker, that with the first contract that goes to a poor old Canadian supplier, the Yanks will be objecting under clause 7 stating that we must renegotiate. Is this parliament going to surrender its right to check on that? We will never know unless somebody squeals to us. Under this legislation, the government does not have to come back to the House. They need only give an innocuous report once a year. I am sure members of this House will not agree to that.
What will happen? When a protest is made, Canadian bids will be reopened. We will have to give the Americans more because they are our big, strong neighbour. We cannot stand up against them. The opposition will never know about it. That is what will happen if we leave this in the shape it is in now.
We in the official opposition want the pipeline, but we want some assurance that it will be constructed properly. We want some assurance that this parliament will be able to check to see that it is done properly. There must be adequate discussion before the bill goes to committee.
If this government is sensible and agrees to the reasonable amendments we suggest, it will be completed in time before the Americans agree to the gas prices, the producers agree to the gas prices and all the rest. Let us not hear that foolish word "unduly" spoken here again for at least a month.
Northern Pipeline
We want a strategy that will give Canada some long-term benefits. The report from industry, trade and commerce states that there will be $226.7 million in Canadian taxes and duties. If the project goes ahead, that is what the government will get. That is the estimate. Some of that money should be used to ensure that Canadian industry gets well established so that we can become foremost in the world with regard to pipeline building, construction, servicing and supplying. When this pipeline is nearly completed, we should be ready to go on to the next one no matter where it is in the world, whether it be in Saudi Arabia or the Carpathian mountains. We should be prepared to do this work, not only protect what we have in Canada.
The government must have an industrial strategy that will take advantage of what comes our way, rather than hiding its head in the sand and prevaricating, as this government has been wont to do.
We have been told that 50 per cent of the content will be Canadian, that no one can interfere with that 50 per cent. No one can stop us having our labourers on the job or using our own gravel and sand. With regard to the other 50 per cent, we are told by the experts that we should concentrate on 35 per cent. I am going by the industry, trade and commerce report and making some suggestions of my own.
We are willing to accept advice from government departments if we think it is wise. What we want is long term industrial benefits. We want what the Science Council has called an industrial strategy for Canada. We want Canadian technological superiority for our northern nation. Our former prime minister had the northern vision which has been so sadly lacking since 1963. Since then we have had nothing but the Liberal vision.

The hon. Leader of the NDP and the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands are taking a wholly impractical position when they indicate that guarantees, with respect to Canadian labour content and industrial content, must be written into the bill.
The hon. member for Yukon continued:

In light of the fact that the agreement calls for implicit understandings ... and refers to bei.ig competitive, and given the fact that the minister has said Canadian interests will be given every opportunity, which means that some room is left open for international bidding, can the minister advise, together with his colleague the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, whether he will see to it that there will be guarantees in order to protect the interests of our steel industry and those who provide goods and services which play a major part in this pipeline?

He was directing a question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and this is again related to what the hon. member for Yukon said last night about sellouts. -my question is for the Prime Minister regarding what I call that great sellout by this government in terms of the northern pipeline and the evasive answers given by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and others. Given the fact that Dr. Stuart Smith, leader of the opposition in the province of Ontario, has indicated by way of a letter to the Prime Minister that he is very, very concerned about this matter-
The hon. member for Hamilton West on that occasion referred to this matter as "that great sellout". 1 am glad to have the views of the hon. member for Hamilton West in this regard on the record, which are contrary to what the hon. member for Yukon had to say last night about this bill.

This would indicate there are at least some Progressive Conservatives who assess this bill as a betrayal or a sellout, and look at the bill as completely lacking
Northern Pipeline
guarantees for Canadian manufacturers of this pipe and Canadian contractors for the pipeline itself.
The hon. member for St. John's West was primarily correct when he said that when the United States government, Congress, decides on an exercise or an enterprise, whether it be public or private, it in fact protects, gives preference to, subsidizes, ensures and guarantees United States manufacturing and labour content.
The Deputy Prime Minister, who is responsible for this bill and was in charge of the negotiations with the United States, behaved in a way that we have seen many times before in the history of our country; his knees trembled, he forgot to keep his back to the wall and his gun loose in his holster. He could have obtained, and I believe still could, guarantees through this legislation, unless the United States wishes to pay an additional $6 billion to $10 billion by going another route. Guarantees to Canadian manufacturing and construction could be written into the legislation. subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-GOVERNMENT PLANS TO CLEAN UP OIL SPILLS
ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-GOVERNMENT PLANS TO CLEAN UP OIL SPILLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, ever since my election in 1974 I have been pressing the Minister of State (Environment) (Mr. Marchand) for an assurance that the Department of the Environment has some kind of operative plan to protect the people of Surrey and White Rock and, as a matter of fact, all the people of the coast of British Columbia, against the future inevitability of a major oil spill.
I recall the spill in 1972 at the Argo plant, and 1 know we are always vulnerable to that kind of disaster off our shores. As a result of that awareness I began pressing the minister, early in October, 1974, for some kind of assurance that there would be contingency plans that would be operative in the case of a major spill. As a matter of fact, I asked the then minister questions so frequently about that particular issue that she became exasperated with me and on one occasion presented me in the House with a computer print-out list of all the equipment in place in Vancouver. That list contained the number of peat bales, booms and so forth, and this surely was a highly irrelevant thing to do.
In November there was a report in one of the Vancouver newspapers under the headline "No government agency capable of major oil cleanup, GVRD told". I had always doubted somewhat the minister's statements to me. When I received that report, I made certain I had a copy of the report which prompted that headline. On January 24, 1978, as reported at page 2176 of Hansard, I asked the following:
In the months of October and November of 1974 I posed a series of questions to the former minister of the environment and asked for the tabling of contingency plans in the event of a major oil spill on the west coast. The former minister assured me, as recorded in Hansard of November 6, 1974, that plans in the Vancouver area were very adequate and, in fact, computerized.
In response to that question, the minister said:
I assure the hon. member that we can deal effectively and quickly with oil spills on the west coast, and on the east coast as well.
I have a copy of the plan which was presented to the GVRD by Mr. Chris Hatfield, the former Pacific region environmental emergency co-ordinator for Environment Canada. This man has credentials and knows what he is talking about. I should like to present to the House some of the items which he mentioned to indicate major deficiencies of contingencies in the GVRD area. The first one reads as follows:
Although all the contingency plans contain much useful information, they are really spill notifications and general policy plans. No site specific action plans are included that describe such things as which local areas have priority for protection or clean up, where field co-ordination centres will be located, or what methods will be used for cleanups in the different areas.
The next item reads as follows:
No comprehensive communications system exists to link all federal government agencies, air and waterborne support, provincial and municipal truck and equipment fleets and contractors together, in order that they may communicate effectively. This results in gross inefficiencies, delays and isolation of many working groups from each other during incidents.
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Ethier).]
It continues by indicating that the Department of National Defence is not included in the contingency plan, although a large body of manpower and communications is available in the event of such an emergency. Another item contained in the plan reads as follows:
Little risk analysis has been carried out in order to give priority in spill control planning to areas having higher exposure to the occurrence of spills. As a result, spills in obvious high risk areas such as Boundary Bay, Vancouver Harbour and Port Moody Arm, are not planned for.
It continues:
No provision has been made for the mock exercise testing of present contingency plans. As a result, when an actual event occurs, details such as telephone lines becoming overloaded, lack of keys for important buildings, or lack of air transport, become critical delay problems.
A few days ago I received a letter from the minister as a result of my urging him to provide some equipment for Surrey and White Rock. The letter indicated that there is a plan for mock exercise some time in 1978, together with American departments. It seems to me that is very indefinite and far too loose. Another indication of a deficiency reads as follows:
There is at present, no provision in current contingency plans for updating. Most existing plans are, therefore, put on shelves, where they become obsolete as personnel and phone numbers change, material suppliers go out of business, and clean-up methods improve.
The closing paragraph of the plan ends on a note of some wry humour. It reads as follows:
To end this section on a positive note, it should be pointed out that the federal government has spared no cost to acquire tremendously sophisticated equipment for communicating information about spills to Ottawa. Any word uttered, picture taken or story printed, can be whisked to Ottawa within milliseconds of its release. Computers, telecopiers, mag card selectric typewriters, telex, multiple speaker telephone conference call hookups and suitcase portable computer access terminals are all used to keep headquarters informed of events-during Ottawa working hours.
[DOT]
The fundamental question is who is in charge in the event of a spill like the one we had in Richmond last summer? We had all the equipment there. The booms, the peat moss and the skimmer were all there, but who is in charge? The final and ultimate question is: Who is going to make the decision to send the equipment out to the site? It looks to me as though we have all kinds of equipment spread along the lower mainland by government departments as well as private industry, but there is no one on site who is the ultimate person in charge and who says, "send it out". As a result, it appears that people are waiting for someone else to do it, and it does not get done.

Ministers responsible for the environment have answered his questions and provided copies of the major contingency plans prepared by departments of the federal government. If the
February 14, 1978

hon. member had read these plans, particularly the joint Canada-United States marine pollution contingency plan, he would realize that the Department of Transport's Canadian Coast Guard is the lead agency for ship originated spills and for those which could affect the Canada-U.S. boundary waters.
