The Department of the Environment has lead agency responsibilities for spills from shore sources which do not affect boundary waters.
At this point I must emphasize that those federal departments that have a duty, or are called upon to respond to spills, do have effective contingency plans. They are exercised in real and in simulated spills, and they do work. Accepting the "polluter pays" principle, our problem is to ensure that potential polluters and other levels of government are equally prepared to respond to spills within their jurisdictions.
The major oil companies and oil spill co-operatives formed under the aegis of PACE, the Petroleum Association for the Conservation of the Canadian Environment, have good contingency plans and have effectively demonstrated their capability to respond to spills for which they are responsible. However, the capabilities of municipal and provincial governments range across Canada from excellent to non-existent. subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-DISINTEGRATION OF SOVIET SATELLITE OVER CANADIAN SOIL-INFORMATION PROVIDED MINISTER
NATIONAL DEFENCE-DISINTEGRATION OF SOVIET SATELLITE OVER CANADIAN SOIL-INFORMATION PROVIDED MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians have reason to be concerned about the security of their nation. Our depleted yet competent military has lost confidence in the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson). The apparent confusion and ineptitude of the minister has been only too well documented in the recent Soviet nuclear powered satellite affair. The Globe and Mail put it very well as follows:
Mr. Danson appears unwilling to complain. Loyal to a fault to his subordinates, he is willing even to make their excuses for them: "The senior actors can be kept out of the picture until they are needed."
Which is utter nonsense. A man who has been kept as completely out of the picture as Mr. Danson obviously was is not a senior actor, or an actor of any sort, except in the role-playing sense. He is, to put it plainly, just a flack.
Adjournment Debate
The final paragraph of the article reads as follows:
How many other pictures is Mr. Danson being kept out of? What else will he know nothing about until it is too late? We know that Russian and American satellites are competing over our heads in a war of spy and counterspy. We know that each side is developing "killer satellites" to knock out the other's space snoopers. Yet the Government of Canada, linked in a defence partnership with the United States, appears content to be left out of the picture-at least until it is needed to explain the next disaster. And Mr. Danson will go on being treated like a flack, until he works up the nerve to stop acting like one.
That is an outside assessment, Mr. Speaker. I could put it more strongly. Canada needs leadership, not the "followship" of the Minister of National Defence. Emergencies require clarity and decision. The recent satellite issue shows that the minister is lacking on both counts. Perhaps the minister should be placed on the back bench until his confusion clears.
The recent communications failure saw the President of the United States providing information to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who, in turn, informed the Minister of National Defence, when the reverse should have been the case. Word should have gone from our Canadian commander to the Minister of National Defence, then to the Prime Minister and then to the President of the United States.
I questioned the former minister in committee regarding the speed and efficiency that would be required for consultation and consolidated defence procedure in emergencies within NORAD that would assure the protection of the sovereignty of the United States and Canada as well as initiate prompt protective measures. The minister's response was that procedures are secure but they are not public. My scepticism at the time has proved unfortunately to be accurate. I want to know what measures the minister has taken to ensure that this communication gap will not occur again. Perhaps the minister should provide an in camera briefing in order that, as representatives of the Canadian people, we can tell them that corrective action has taken place to assure their security to the maximum degree possible in spite of the imperfections of the minister and his "busy" systems.
Perhaps since the Prime Minister as well as the Minister of National Defence failed to grasp the significance of Canada's participation in NORAD, that does in fact give Canada access to United States space surveillance information and points to the fact that parliament, and in particular the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, needs further briefings on the purpose and functioning of NORAD. Will the minister refer this matter to that committee for further study and investigation?
I want a strong, secure Canada. Since Canada cannot defend itself I want our ties with our allies in NORAD and NATO resecured and strengthened. I know we have time-tested friends within these agreements, and perhaps through discussions we might even determine if there really is any threat or enemy and, if so, who that threat and enemy is and where they are. I asked the former minister of national defence and the former secretary of state for external affairs who our enemies are, and neither could tell me.

February 14, 1978
Adjournment Debate
Can the present minister tell us who the enemies are that we are defending ourselves against? Where is the threat? Has he told us in a recent statement, where he declared that the Soviet Union had a grand plan to impose its will on Canadians by force if they were unsuccessful through non-violent methods? Quite frankly, I do not think even the minister believes that, or does he? Can we take his word or is this ministerial irresponsibility again? Or is it just one more government deception as a decadent and crumbling government makes one last desperate grasp for power; as it attempts to give three loud cheers for the constitution, three more for the United States and the RCMP, and three kisses and boos for the Russians, the spendthrift provinces and the opposition?
When the minister-or whatever hon. flack the minister has chosen to respond to me tonight-stands to answer my question, let him address the issue, identify our internal and external enemies and assure us that we have taken corrective procedures for the security of Canada. Let us recognize that while in the short term we will have to rely on strengthening our defences through NATO and NORAD, in the longer term these are but functionary vehicles currently possessed of the evil of confusion and power lust.
The real danger and enemies of this world are hate, anger, fear, bigotry, selfishness and perverted violence in whatever vehicle or in whatever place or person or country they might be found. Let us recognize that our defence against these enemies must be attacked first by individuals with an inner strength of spirit, of love, peace, truth and natural justice, acting without fear and with courage and clarity. Let these be the common values that will unite Canadians with a will and a way to build a nation that is worth defending.
I call now on the person chosen to speak on behalf of the minister to stand and speak strongly and clearly and to assure this nation that we are secure.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jacques Guilbault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-DISINTEGRATION OF SOVIET SATELLITE OVER CANADIAN SOIL-INFORMATION PROVIDED MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is probably because we are nearing election time that my friend and colleague from Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman) has the inspiration to make a speech such as we have just heard, which is more or less an election speech we would normally hear in the public forum once hostilities between political parties have started. There must be special circumstances indeed when a very secondary event reported in the newspaper, namely the contention that the minister and the chief of defence staff were not quite in contact, leads to such diatribes.
For my part, I find myself in a privileged position as parliamentary secretary to the minister to know exactly of the close ties which exist between the minister and his departmental officials. 1 find absolutely groundless the contentions of my hon. friend to the effect that the minister does not play an important role in defence, in Canada, and that he is removed from his officials. To prove him wrong, I shall read a document that was given to me by the officials, and which only

serves to prove that they maintain very close relationships with the minister and his parliamentary secretary.

In response to the hon. member's question in the House on January 30, 1978, concerning lines of communication between himself and the chief of defence staff with regard to information on Cosmos 954, the minister stated that they were in constant communication and were working in close concert, and any difference on the information given was that of timing.
It was and is the minister's wish that information on events concerning the Cosmos 954 be given freely as they occur. The contradictions of information outlined by the hon. member did not, in fact, take place. At a briefing just prior to the minister's departure for Toronto on the Friday afternoon of January 27, 1978, both he and Admiral Falls, the chief of defence staff, were advised that a significant "hot spot" had been detected. This information remained unchanged until just five minutes before Admiral Falls' scheduled press conference at 3.30 p.m. the same day, at a time when the minister was airborne enroute to Toronto.
In accordance with the minister's instruction, Admiral Falls properly proceeded with his press conference, in which he disclosed that the hot spot was not confirmed. This information was relayed to the minister when his aircraft landed in Toronto.
That is the sense and the gist of this whole big event that the hon. member is trying to blow up into immense proportions. In reality the minister and the senior members of the defence staff are constantly working together, and I know of no other civil servants who work in a comparable fashion respecting the authority of the minister than those we have in the defence staff.

Mr. Speaker, on December 8 I asked the minister about requesting aid for the plastics industry. He said at that time that he felt the 10 per cent discount on our dollar would be of sufficient help and that we would be using our own raw materials.
When I asked about cutting interest rates and cutting capital aid, he said that Treasury Board would have to pay for this. Well, that is the taxpayer of Canada. That means all Canadians who are now paying for about one million unemployed. I leave it to reasoned judgment which we would prefer.
I want to speak about the economic mismanagement of this government. Our industry has gradually priced itself out of world markets. Our exports of manufactured goods have fallen simply because of the burden of increased taxes on labour and management. This burden could not be met without increasing the price of the article that was manufactured and paying more to labour to meet the demands of inflation and increased taxation.
February 14, 1978

I do not believe anyone would seriously argue with me the incompetency of the present government in the economic debate. Perhaps I would not be too unkind if I said that it is the most incompetent of all governments in its field since confederation. As an example, let us compare what it has done in the labour field. A Canadian workman would probably receive SI per hour more than his American counterpart. However, because of our heavy taxation the American has more take-home pay. In addition, his living costs are 15 per cent less. Added to this is the fact that his dollar is worth 10 per cent more.
No wonder we are selling less and less goods outside of Canada. A reduction in tariff protection in Canada would endanger some industries. I speak of the plastic industry in particular. If present conditions are allowed to exist, with government taxation at an all-time high, a million unemployed and a high inflation rate, this country will keep on losing its exports markets and factories. For this reason industries are leaving Canada almost weekly.
Many industries have moved out of the province of Quebec into the New England states and Vermont, where labour earns less but people are employed because the production can be sold. They also have more take-home pay which enables them to purchase more goods and services.
This is the situation in the plastics industry today. There are 1,400 manufacturing establishments, a market of around $2.6 billion, one-third supplied by imports. The industry input goes into various markets. About 150 pounds of plastics go into an automobile. By 1982 or 1983, it is estimated that this will be up to 550 pounds. Plastics represent 6 per cent of the manufacturing components of Canada's gross national product. The plastics industry employs directly nearly 50,000 people and has increased its employment 6 per cent per year up until last year.
The general need is to be internationally competitive. That is impossible if protection is not given or incentive programs such as tax credits are not used in every way possible to stimulate productivity and efficiency.
This situation is now more acute. Petrosar at Sarnia is turning Alberta oil and gas into petroschemicals, into pellets used by plastics fabricators, and into a growing list of products such as insulation, pipes, drains, cups and so on. If conditions are not made more favourable, most of the petrochemicals will be exported and we will be buying back from those companies our manufactured articles.
1 appeal to the minister. He knows full well that Canada is the largest importer of plastics per capita in the world. Canada imports more plastics products than any other country in the world, more than the United States which has ten times our population. Does the minister fully realize that Canada imports more finished products per capita than any country in the world and that our total deficit trade balance in manufactured goods in 1976 amounted to $10.2 billion, roughly equivalent to 500,000 jobs?
Adjournment Debate
In the absence of a manufacturing industry the role of the risk-taker disappears. Unless changes are introduced along the lines I have outlined, our only role would be that of an exporter of natural resources, thus admitting to the world that the government, and we as parliamentarians, cannot make the grade. Well, Mr. Speaker, I have seen too many smart Canadians holding top jobs south of the border to listen to that lament. What have we got to offer? In the absence of manufacturing, research will dry up. And that is progress in reverse.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bernard Loiselle (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our department has co-operated closely with the main association of the plastics industry, the Association of Plastics Industries, and the provincial governments, to make an in-depth study of the plastics industry in Canada. This study aimed at identifying the problems and the potentials of the industry in the next few years.
The main facts are as follows: Between 1964 and 1974, the industry's part of the total production of manufacturing industries increased from 3 per cent to 6 per cent; it should be noted that this pattern is expected to continue. Indeed, it is anticipated that between 1975 and 1985, the demand for plastic products will increase on the average by 10 per cent a year, which is a much higher rate of growth than for the entire sector of manufacturing industries.
Because of its high rate of growth, it is not surprising that this sector has all the characteristics of a youthful and inexperienced industry, including fragmentation, overly rapid development and underutilization of its facilities. These negative factors have forced the Canadian plastics industry to suffer higher losses than its American counterpart.
Study of this sector shows that capital expenses excluded, the difference in costs is of about 15 per cent and that if we take into account the difference in capital costs, the difference is 2.5 per cent to 3 per cent more. It should be underlined that this analysis is based on equivalence between Canadian and American currencies. The major factor in the difference in costs is the fact that raw materials required for the manufacture of plastic resin are more expensive in Canada. When petrochemical complexes are opened in Alberta, Ontario and Quebec, this will considerably increase the Canadian plastic resin production capacity. The Canadian price of resin is already becoming increasingly competitive with that of the United States and other international markets; this may result from the implementation of a more energetic marketing policy by Canadian resin producers who anticipated the opening of these new facilities.
Fragmentation and overcapacity constitute the other factors which explain the cost differential between Canadian and American industries. It is very difficult to solve this problem because of the high rate of demand for plastic products, of the relatively low costs of the addition of new facilities in anticipation of an increase in the demand and of the ease with which new manufacturers can enter that industry. It will have to play a prominent role if it becomes necessary to reduce the costs

February 14, 1978
Adjournment Debate
brought about by its overcapacity. It will have to carry out more thorough studies to determine if new facilities are needed before building them.
The department and the Association of Plastics Industries also believe that it would be useful to carry out a certain regrouping within that industry through mergers and agreements calling for specialization; they are actually now getting prepared to study this issue in a more detailed manner.
It is worth noting that the department and the Association of Plastics Industries' will look for means to increase Canadian exports of plastic goods particularly to the United States; this will be another way to enhance the efficiency of that industry. The tariffs applied to plastic products entering the United States are relatively low and could again be reduced through GATT negotiations now under way. The creation of export consortiums and the use of better technology for export development will also be studied.
The Canadian plastics industry is one of the sectors in Canada which has experienced the most rapid growth; in that
respect, prospects are excellent for the coming decade. If prices of raw materials get closer to those of American industries, if we use our plants in a more rational manner, if we set appropriate Canadian tariffs and if we facilitate the access to foreign markets, particularly the United States, and if we get a favourable exchange rate, this sector of the Canadian industry will be able to expand so as to meet the very high demand for plastic products which will exist in Canada by the year 1985. For that purpose, it will be necessary to reduce inasmuch as possible, disparities between costs; furthermore, the industry and the government will have to work more closely. We believe that at the present time, only the first steps have been made in that direction and we hope to have permanent and fruitful discussions with the representatives from this industry.
